old: Figure~\ref{fig:decerebrate_cat} shows what that accounting leaves out. The image is a frame from footage of a real decerebrate-cat experiment, the class of preparation on which the field's understanding of spinal locomotion has been built since its beginnings \citep{brown_intrinsic_1911, decerebrate_cat_footage}: a living cat, its forebrain disconnected by a brainstem transection, walks on the treadmill because the neurons distal to the laceration are still living, still connected, and still firing action potentials. The published record of this work is drawn almost exclusively in schematic, labeled boxes for half-centers and color-coded reflex arcs that are honest about the circuitry and silent about the animal. The figure is included as the counterweight, documenting what the experiments looked like, and therefore what a replacement method stands in for.
new: Schematics of decerebrate-cat locomotion emphasize the neural circuits under study, but often leave the surgical preparation out of view. A simplified drawing of a walking cat can make the animal appear intact, alert, or even contented. That appearance should not be confused with the condition of the experimental animal: a brainstem transection has disconnected the forebrain, while neural circuits below the transection can still generate treadmill stepping \citep{brown_intrinsic_1911, severin_1967}. Figure~\ref{fig:decerebrate_cat}, taken from archival footage, shows the physical preparation behind the circuit diagrams \citep{decerebrate_cat_footage}. This distinction makes the ethical meaning of replacement concrete: the robotic experiments discussed here are intended to reproduce selected neural mechanisms without repeating these invasive preparations in living animals.

old: The procedures behind that record are documented in films that remain publicly available.
new: The contrast between an intact animal and the experimental preparation is particularly clear in publicly available teaching footage.
